Marine ecosystems worldwide are subject to intensifying and increasingly cumulative anthropogenic pressure, arising from fishing, shipping, resource extraction, pollution, and climate-driven change, with coastal and shelf waters bearing the highest combined impact [@halpernGlobalMapHuman2008; @halpernSpatialTemporalChanges2015]. Conserving marine biodiversity under these pressures depends on the capacity to detect where species occur and how their distributions shift, which requires monitoring that is systematic, spatially explicit, and repeatable [@damenClimateChangeCetacean2025]. Large-bodied, upper-trophic predators are both disproportionately exposed to these pressures and unusually informative about the state of the systems they occupy, and have accordingly been adopted as sentinels of marine ecosystem condition [@gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @mannocciAssessingCetaceanSurveys2018].

Among marine megafauna, cetaceans are widely regarded as indicator species for marine ecosystem health [REF]. As apex predators, they integrate ecological pressures across multiple trophic levels and broad spatial scales, such that their distribution and abundance can serve as reliable proxies for the condition of the ecosystems they inhabit [@hammondEstimatingAbundanceMarine2021; @mannocciAssessingCetaceanSurveys2018; @forliImpactTouristicWhalewatching2024]. Robust, spatially explicit knowledge of cetacean occurrence is therefore a prerequisite for effective marine spatial planning and for the design and evaluation of conservation measures.

The Strait of Gibraltar is among the most ecologically significant and heavily trafficked marine corridors globally. As the sole connection between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, it supports a diverse cetacean community [@stephanisSummerSpatialDistribution2008; @canales-caceresDistributionBehaviourStriped2023; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @olaya-ponzoneSpatioTemporalPatternsLimited2026], and its importance is formally recognised through designation as an Important Marine Mammal Area (IMMA) by the IUCN Marine Mammal Protected Areas Task Force [@SummaryCurrentIMMAs], contiguous with the Atlantic Coast of the Iberian Peninsula IMMA. The regional assemblage is dominated by delphinids: short-beaked common dolphins (*Delphinus delphis*), striped dolphins (*Stenella coeruleoalba*), and common bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops truncatus*), alongside seasonal occurrence of larger cetaceans, including fin whales (*Balaenoptera physalus*) migrating between the Atlantic and Mediterranean [@canales-caceresDistributionBehaviourStriped2023; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @olaya-ponzoneMixedspeciesDolphinGroups2025] (@fig-species).

![Cetaceans present in the study area: short-beaked common dolphin (*Delphinus delphis*, A), striped dolphin (*Stenella coeruleoalba*, B), and fin whaless (*Balaenoptera physalus*, C).](/misc/intro_dolph.png){#fig-species}

The conservation stakes in this region are high. The Mediterranean subpopulation of common dolphin is classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List [@IUCNUK20121RLTST134817215A195829089en1], having undergone a marked decline over recent decades, and the adjacent Alboran Sea holds the largest concentration of the subpopulation in the Mediterranean [@SummaryCurrentIMMAs]. The Mediterranean fin whale, also recorded here, was recently reassessed from Vulnerable to Endangered [@disciaraBalaenopteraPhysalusMediterranean]. Robust distribution and density data for these species within heavily trafficked corridors are therefore directly relevant to their conservation.

The British Gibraltar Territorial Waters (BGTW) form a small, bounded body of water at the western entrance to the Mediterranean, encompassing the waters around the Gibraltar peninsula and the eastern Bay of Gibraltar. Despite their limited extent, these waters lie at the confluence of the Strait's Atlantic–Mediterranean exchange and one of the busiest shipping and bunkering areas in the region, subjecting resident and transiting cetaceans to intense vessel traffic, anchorage activity, and associated disturbance (@fig-studyarea). This combination of high ecological value and concentrated anthropogenic pressure, within a jurisdictionally bounded territory, makes the BGTW both a conservation priority and a tractable unit for systematic survey.

![The British Gibraltar Territorial Waters (BGTW) surrounding the Gibraltar peninsula, showing the full study area divided into three strata (East, South, and West).](/figures/bgtw_map.png){#fig-studyarea}

A structured review of cetacean distribution research in the Western Mediterranean (Supplementary Material) situates this study within the existing literature. Research effort in the region is substantial but conducted overwhelmingly at regional or basin scale. For example through habitat-based distribution modelling and the large-scale line-transect programmes of the Agreement on the Conservation of Cetaceans of the Black Sea, Mediterranean Sea and contiguous Atlantic area (ACCOBAMS) Survey Initiative [@canadasModelbasedAbundanceEstimates2023; @panigadaACCOBAMSSurveyInitiative2024], with fine-scale, design-based coverage of the Bay of Gibraltar and the BGTW largely absent. Methodologically, this effort is dominated by vessel-based line-transect and photo-identification approaches, while land-based survey remains comparatively rare [@giacomaAreLandBased2013; @gutierrez-munozPatternsTrendsCetacean2021].

Consistent with this, cetacean occurrence within the BGTW has not been documented by a dedicated systematic survey. Existing local knowledge derives almost entirely from opportunistic and photo-identification records [@olaya-ponzonePhotoIdentificationCatalogueDelphinus2025; @olaya-ponzoneMixedspeciesDolphinGroups2025; @bamfordAnalysisDorsalEdge2016]. Approaches that, while valuable for establishing species presence, are subject to substantial spatial and temporal bias and cannot yield reliable estimates of density or distribution [@bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001; @dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008]. This absence of design-based data constitutes a two-fold gap, of place and of method, within a bounded, heavily utilised territory of high conservation relevance.

Distance sampling offers a rigorous, effort-corrected framework for addressing this gap, estimating density and distribution from systematically collected sighting data rather than inferring them from presence records alone [@bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001; @bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015; @thomasDistanceSoftwareDesign2010]. It is among the most widely applied methods for estimating cetacean abundance and distribution and underpins large-scale systematic surveys by bodies including the International Whaling Commission (IWC), ACCOBAMS, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) [@dickUsingDistanceSampling2011a; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @raudinoAerialAbundanceEstimates2023]. These applications are overwhelmingly vessel-based, most often via shipboard line transects [@dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008; @lerczakCalculatingSightingDistances1998]; the method can, however, be adapted to shore-based observation, offering a low-cost, non-invasive alternative well suited to bounded coastal waters where vessel access is constrained.

The present study applies this shore-based adaptation to provide the first systematic assessment of cetacean distribution and relative density within the BGTW, and to evaluate systematic survey against the existing opportunistic record. Specifically, it aimed to (1) characterise cetacean species composition, spatial distribution, and relative density within the BGTW using systematic distance sampling; (2) compare systematic and opportunistic survey outputs to evaluate the relative value of each monitoring approach; and (3) assess the adequacy of existing conservation measures and propose evidence-based recommendations for the territory.
